# Running the notebooks {#sec-running}

## Three ways to use this companion

1. **Read the website.** The sliders (OJS panels) run in the browser with no installation. Open `_book/index.html`
   through a web server (e.g. `quarto preview`, or any static host such as GitHub Pages or the university web space).
   Some browsers block the interactive panels when the file is opened directly from disk.
2. **Run the code in Jupyter.** Each chapter exists as a notebook in `notebooks/` (generated with
   `quarto convert chapter.qmd`). The notebook `notebooks/interactive_explorers.ipynb` gathers **ipywidgets**
   versions of the main panels (fiber designer, b–V chart, dispersion, link simulator).
3. **Rebuild the book** after editing a chapter.

## Publishing the website (GitHub Pages)

The source lives at <https://github.com/{{< var github_user >}}/{{< var repo >}}> and the site at
<https://{{< var github_user >}}.github.io/{{< var repo >}}/>. After editing a chapter:

```bash
cd notebooks && python build_notebooks.py && cd ..   # refresh the notebooks (Colab buttons point to them)
git add -A && git commit -m "Update chapter" && git push   # update the source on GitHub
quarto publish gh-pages                                  # render and update the website
```

## Installation

```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt     # numpy scipy matplotlib pandas jupyter ipywidgets (+ optional OptiCommPy)
quarto preview                      # live preview while editing
quarto render                       # builds _book/ (HTML)
```

Rendering executes every Python cell once. Results are cached in `_freeze/` (`freeze: auto`), so later builds only
re-run the chapters you changed.

## Regenerating the notebooks

```bash
cd notebooks
python build_notebooks.py
```

The script converts every chapter, adds a setup cell that works both locally and in Colab (it downloads
`fiberlib.py` from GitHub when running in Colab), and rebuilds `interactive_explorers.ipynb`.

The notebooks keep the Python cells. The OJS cells (browser panels) appear as non-executable cells. Use
`interactive_explorers.ipynb` for their Python equivalents.

## The `fiberlib` module

| function | purpose |
|---|---|
| `slab_modes`, `slab_field`, `slab_penetration`, `slab_beta` | symmetric planar guide, TE/TM |
| `LP_b`, `LP_all`, `LP_count`, `LP_field`, `b_approx` | step-index LP modes (exact, weak guidance) |
| `mfd_marcuse`, `mfd_exact_gaussian`, `mfd_petermann2` | mode-field diameter |
| `n_doped`, `n_silica`, `group_index`, `D_material` | Sellmeier glasses and material dispersion |
| `neff_smf`, `group_delay_smf`, `D_total_smf`, `D_waveguide_approx` | exact chromatic dispersion of an SMF |
| `sigma_intermodal_grin` | Olshansky–Keck graded-index spread |
| `rayleigh_alpha`, `attenuation_model` | loss |
| `prbs`, `imdd_link`, `eye_metrics`, `Q_to_BER` | link simulation |
| `fbg_reflectance`, `fbg_bandwidth`, `fabry_perot_T` | gratings and interferometers |

Every function was checked against the worked examples of the slides (see the "recomputed" sections).
